title: Kahana vs Skool: Discovery Beside the LMS
excerpt: Skool is simple community + classroom: group feed, courses, and gamification for cohort-style creator communities. Kahana is discovery + cohort discussion around teaching you already run elsewhere.

columns.label: Ebook
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily get and consume ebooks on the platform (free or paid) as a first-class product, open, buy, borrow, or read without hunting.

columns.label: Short-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily consume short-form video as a first-class surface (For You, Reels, Shorts).

columns.label: Long-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch creator / UGC long-form video (or specialty long video) as a core surface. Course lectures belong under Courses. Hollywood catalogs belong under Series/Films.

columns.label: Series/Films
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch series and films as an SVOD / catalog entertainment product.

columns.label: Courses
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily take or browse structured courses as a first-class product.

columns.label: Newsletters
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily read or subscribe to newsletters / creator writing as a first-class product.

columns.label: Audio
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily listen to music, podcasts, or audiobooks as a first-class product.

columns.label: Memberships
columns.definition: Yes if a creator or seller can accept payments from others and make money through the platform, checkout, fan subscriptions, tips, ads, shop, or creator funds. Not only a classic Patreon-style membership product.

columns.label: Community & Messaging
columns.definition: Yes if you can create or join a group, community, or club, including group chats, Groups, subreddits, community tabs, discussion boards, or community feeds. A one-off comment on a single video or listing is not the bar; a durable place for the group to talk is.

columns.label: Storefronts
columns.definition: Yes if the product gives a creator a custom storefront or site that can take the place of building their own website (bio page, creator site, branded shop). Not a shop tab on someone else’s multi-seller marketplace.

columns.label: Marketplaces
columns.definition: Yes if a typical person can search and shop a catalog of offerings from many sellers, courses, books, digital goods, etc. Storefront software (Shopify, WooCommerce) is not a marketplace unless shoppers browse many sellers there.

scaleFacts: Specific user and revenue numbers are not widely disclosed; Skool is a newer, fast-growing platform.
Hobby plan at USD 9/month for low-friction entry; main creator plans add processing and transaction fees.
Targets online coaches, course creators, masterminds, accountability groups, and free/paid memberships.

strengths.title: Integrated courses + community + live events
strengths.detail: Host courses, chats, meetups, and webinars in one platform, less need for Zoom + Discord + a separate course tool.

strengths.title: Gamification and engagement
strengths.detail: Points, levels, and leaderboards help drive activity and a more lively community.

strengths.title: Simple, friendly UX
strengths.detail: Clean interface that is easy for admins and members to navigate.

strengths.title: Affordable entry pricing
strengths.detail: Hobby plan (~USD 9/month) makes it easy to try; generally affordable for small communities aside from transaction fees.

weaknesses.title: Limited course features
weaknesses.detail: Fine for simple delivery, but weak on quizzes, certificates, assignments, and detailed progress tracking.

weaknesses.title: No built-in funnels or landing pages
weaknesses.detail: No robust funnel/landing builder; native checkout is simple, limited marketing control for advanced sellers.

weaknesses.title: No native automation builder
weaknesses.detail: Unlike Circle or Kajabi, no built-in workflows for triggers, tagging, onboarding, or segmentation.

weaknesses.title: Limited native integrations
weaknesses.detail: Weak direct email/CRM/automation integrations; creators often rely on Zapier or similar.

content:
Kahana is a library of curated hubs, Explore, Clubs, and optional Stripe. Skool is simple community + classroom: group feed, courses, and gamification for cohort-style creator communities. They overlap in places and diverge in others.

What each one is

Kahana is built around hubs people can open, Explore so strangers can find them, Aura as scarce daily recognition, and Clubs so discussion outlives a feed. Selling stays optional.

Skool is a platform to sell online courses and host community at the same time, courses, community chats, live meetups, and webinars in one place.

Why this comparison

This article puts Kahana and Skool side by side. It covers what each supports as a first-class product job, key features, and a few research notes so you have a clearer picture of what they are, how they compare, and what you can actually do on each one. It is not a teardown, and it is not a switch-tomorrow pitch.
contentAfter:
What you can do on each

On Kahana you can publish a hub, list it on Explore, discuss it in a Club, grant Aura, and turn on a Stripe paywall when you are ready to charge.

On Skool you can use Courses, Memberships, and Community & Messaging as first-class product jobs. You are running a full course engine: drip, quizzes, student progress, and checkout that already works.

Using Kahana with Skool

You can use both. Skool keeps doing what it already does well. Kahana is another place to package the work, get discovered, and grow an audience.

Keep the course engine on Skool for drip, quizzes, and enrollment. Also list or link that teaching on Kahana so Explore, Clubs, and Aura can give it another place to be found. Skool stays the LMS; Kahana is another surface for exposure.
